supported_cases.tutor_answer: In round robin scheduling, each ready process is given a fixed time quantum to execute on the CPU. This means the scheduler allocates a predetermined, equal slice of processor time to every process in the ready queue. When a process's time quantum expires, the running process is moved to the back of the ready queue, allowing the next process in line to receive its own quantum. This creates a fair, cyclic rotation among all ready processes.

supported_cases.tutor_answer: First come first served (FCFS) scheduling runs ready processes in the order they arrive. The convoy effect is caused by a long CPU burst in FCFS scheduling: because processes run strictly in arrival order, a single long-running job holds the CPU and delays all shorter jobs that arrived after it, making them wait in a 'convoy' behind it. By contrast, round robin scheduling avoids this by giving each ready process a fixed time quantum; when the quantum expires, the running process is sent to the back of the ready queue, so no single process can monopolize the CPU for an extended period.

supported_cases.query: How does a mutex protect a critical section?
supported_cases.tutor_answer: A race condition occurs when the result of a program depends on the interleaving of concurrent accesses to shared data. This is the problem a mutex is designed to prevent. A mutex protects a critical section by allowing only one thread to enter at a time. In other words, when a thread acquires the mutex, no other thread can enter the protected region until the first thread releases it, eliminating the harmful interleaving that causes race conditions.
